context: a letter from J. D. Hooker, which you are answering
exchanges:
It is a age since we corresponded. I have been engrossed morning noon & night with business. My father has been away, he is much shaken, though quite as well as, at his age, can be expected. My Herbm. Clerk died last week, a most serious loss to me, as he knew the ins & outs of the establishment from childhood, & was so trusty accurate & dependable: he was son of old Smith.

Now we have to get rid of Curator of Pleasure Grounds, & I want to take advantage of this to reorganize the whole establishment, which is worked to death, & I dread a break down of our new Curator, who, what with Garden duties & accounts, works 16 hours a day: as for myself who have never done less, this is all very well, but persons not accustomed to it cannot stand it— as matters stand neither he nor I could leave Kew a week.

Then all Burchell’s enormous collections have come here, & I have not only to train a new Clerk for myself, but a new Herbarium assistant— Oliver’s defect is, that he is not a good utilizer of others labor, which is a sad draw-back both on his own acct:, & that of others, as he fails to train those under him & me.

I am trying to look my future fairly in the face, but cannot see far ahead. My dear old Father piles duty on duty, & will neither give in nor give up. I do admire his gallantry, & I do not want to see him give up, but things do get into dreadful confusion, & I shall have a heavy day of reckoning

I send 2 letters of Willys which refresh me wonderfully— the complexity of blunders is charming.

Lyell has sent me p. 112 of Principles to look over (Ch. VII. on changes of temperature)   much of the detailed argument seems to me a blunder altogether & that he is out of his depth. I should like to talk it over with you   Have you read Tylors book on Prehistoric man? I am charmed with it—& rather disappointed with Lubbocks. I wish he had not reclamated in re Lyell, whether right or wrong.

My wife is poorly— I hoped she was to have given me a little daughter 7 months hence but she seems in an ambiguous way. Pray say nothing of it in writing to me—

Ever yr affec | J D Hooker

I am heartily sorry to hear that you are so overworked: I suppose you cannot avoid it; but it really is enough to kill you.— Anyhow do not write to me; for I know better than you can tell me that you would very often write (& how often you have written) to amuse me if you were only quarter idle.—

I return Willie’s letters; there is something very charming in their simplicity & the Latin is splenditious; but I am not a “bonus latinus”.—

I have had a shocking month with much sickness & have done nothing: I am now trying, at first with strong hope, now with weak hope, Dr. Chapman’s ice-bags along the spine, which at least is comfortable.—

I do not quite agree about Lubbock; or at least it would have been extraordinary generous to suffer the imputation of copying whole sentences from Lyell, without any acknowlegment.— The passage in Lubbock, when I first read it made my blood grow cold, & I think, if I were in Lyell’s place I would not publish again: his memory must have failed him for the time.—

I have not seen Tylor; but it is my great misery that I can hardly read a page without my head being affected. Some of Lubbock’s book has been read aloud to me & I like it very much: he writes admirably I think.

My dear old friend | Yours affect, | C. Darwin

Our children enjoyed their visit to Kew much.—

P.S. Did you ever see a peloric Antirrhinum majus: if not, perhaps you wd. like to see enclosed. I bought a plant & fertilised it with own pollen & every seedling is peloric as enclosed one,—all with 6 sepals, 6 divisions to corolla & 6 stamens.— From what Lindley says on Order, it seems rather odd that they are none of them pentamerous.—

I have received a correspondence from Lyell this morning with Lubbock.— It is most unfortunate. Lubbock ought, I think, to have given in full Lyell’s explanation. No doubt Lyell took & forgot whole sentences from Lubbock— It is horrid— It will be our turn some day—perhaps we two shall tear each other’s eyes out some day. I begin to think that an author had better be kicked or spat upon rather than reclaim!
